meta.title: Who really said "Time and tide wait for no man"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Chaucer. He wrote “Ay fleeth the tyme; it nyl no man abyde” — no “tide.” The time-and-tide proverb is anonymous, documented from the 1500s.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Time and tide wait for no man'?
meta.ogDescription: Chaucer gets the credit, but he never paired time with tide. The proverb is an anonymous English saying recorded across the 16th–18th centuries.

answer.label: Not Geoffrey Chaucer — an anonymous English proverb
answer.authorDates: Documented in English from the 16th century; near-modern wording by 1764
answer.sourceLine: Chaucer is routinely credited, but the line he actually wrote — “Ay fleeth the tyme; it nyl no man abyde” (Prologue to the Clerk’s Tale, c. 1395) — is about time fleeing and never mentions “tide.” The familiar “time and tide” proverb is anonymous: it takes shape over centuries — “The tide tarrieth no man” (Heywood, 1546), “time nor tide tarrieth no man” (Greene, 1592), “time and tide (that staies for no man)” (Nashe, 1596) — before the near-modern “time and tide waits for no Man” wording appears by 1764, and the exact “wait for no man” phrasing is attested by 1857.

source.heading: What Chaucer actually wrote

docMeta.dd: “Ay fleeth the tyme; it nyl no man abyde” — Clerk’s Prologue, c. 1395

source.excerpt: For thogh we slepe, or wake, or rome, or ryde, / Ay fleeth the tyme; it nyl no man abyde.
trail: Chaucer’s actual couplet reads “Ay fleeth the tyme; it nyl no man abyde” — time only, no tide; the chronology at Random Idea English notes he does not use the word “tide” at all.
The “time and tide” pairing is documented later: “The tide tarrieth no man” (Heywood, 1546) and “Time nor tide tarrieth no man” (Greene, 1592), per Idiom Origins.
Phrases.org.uk traces the oldest “time and tide” record to St Marher (1225) and calls the exact origin uncertain — it does not credit Chaucer.
Wiktionary’s earliest cited uses of the full modern phrase are Dickens’s Little Dorrit (1857) and Wodehouse (1903) — centuries after Chaucer, and with no attribution to him.
source.excerptNote: Chaucer’s genuine line, from the Prologue to the Clerk’s Tale (c. 1395). It says time flees and waits for no man — but it never pairs time with “tide,” which is the distinctive feature of the modern proverb.
source.rightsNote: The wording is a traditional English proverb with no single author. Its modern form is documented well before 1931 — e.g. Arthur Murphy’s The Apprentice (1764) and Dickens’s Little Dorrit (1857) — and Chaucer’s ancestral line dates to c. 1395, so all attested forms are in the public domain.

author.name: Geoffrey Chaucer
author.heading: Why Chaucer gets the credit
author.metaLine: c. 1343–1400 · English poet, author of The Canterbury Tales
author.bio: Chaucer, the medieval poet behind The Canterbury Tales, is the name most often attached to “time and tide wait for no man.” The reason is a real but different line: in the Prologue to the Clerk’s Tale he writes “Ay fleeth the tyme; it nyl no man abyde” — time flees and waits for no one. But that couplet contains no “tide,” and the alliterative proverb we quote today is an anonymous English saying that his verse merely anticipates in spirit.

cite.sourceCitation: Geoffrey Chaucer, “The Clerk’s Prologue,” in The Canterbury Tales (c. 1395), for the line “Ay fleeth the tyme; it nyl no man abyde.” The proverb “time and tide wait for no man” is anonymous: the “time and tide” pairing is recorded from Robert Greene, A Disputation (1592), with the near-modern “waits for no man” wording by Arthur Murphy, The Apprentice (1764).

misattribution.heading: The Chaucer mix-up
misattribution.intro: Chaucer earns the credit because he wrote a genuinely famous line about time not waiting — but the proverb everyone quotes is a different, anonymous saying that adds “tide.”

items.why: Chaucer’s real line is “Ay fleeth the tyme; it nyl no man abyde” (Clerk’s Prologue, c. 1395) — time only, no “tide.” The detailed chronology notes he is “often credited” but never pairs time with tide.

items.who: “Tyme and tide tarie no man” as Chaucer’s words
items.why: Some sites print a pseudo-Middle-English “Chaucer” version. The “time nor tide tarrieth no man” form actually belongs to Robert Greene’s Disputation (1592), not Chaucer, per Idiom Origins.

misattribution.truthLine: “Time and tide wait for no man” is an anonymous English proverb that built up over centuries — Heywood (1546), Greene (1592), Nashe (1596) — reaching its modern wording by 1764, as the documented timeline shows.

context.heading: Why “tide” is not what you think
lead: The proverb sounds like it warns against the sea, but when the “time and tide” pairing took hold, tide still carried its older sense of “a season” or “a while” — the same root that survives in Yuletide and Whitsuntide. Time and tide were near-synonyms, and the doubling was largely for alliterative force.

That is also why the line reads as a genuine folk proverb rather than a single writer’s coinage: it survives because it sounds good, and it accreted its wording across many hands over some four hundred years.
context.pull: Chaucer wrote that time waits for no man. The “tide” belongs to everyone and no one.
